current_answer: Young-worker entry can weaken in AI-exposed work without proving that AI-using firms caused the decline. In a Danish survey linked to records through December 2024, the early-career share in 11 exposed occupations fell, but workplaces encouraging chatbot use showed no extra decline relative to other workplaces; the authors rule out a difference larger than about one-third of a percentage point. This is another result from a study already in our ledger, not a new replication. It does not erase U.S. graduate and hiring warnings or a later 41-country affiliate study that uses a different adoption proxy. U.S. factory AI-skill ads still show higher advertised pay, not worker raises. None of these findings predicts your own job.

catalogue_card.question: Did AI-using firms cause the junior-job slide?
catalogue_card.text: A Danish study found no extra early-career-share decline at workplaces encouraging chatbots through 2024. It cannot settle U.S. or later hiring risks.

summary: Early-career share fell in AI-exposed Danish occupations, but workplaces encouraging chatbots showed no extra decline through December 2024.
This is a result from an already tracked study, not a second independent study or proof that AI never affects hiring.
U.S. graduate-entry warnings and later multinational affiliate evidence use other groups, dates and adoption measures; direct attribution remains unsettled.
uncertainty: The Danish comparison covers selected occupations and data through December 2024; employer encouragement is not randomized AI adoption.
The Danish null does not identify why its exposed occupations lost early-career share or settle U.S. and later multinational findings.
The Brookings article presents the same underlying Danish study already tracked, not an independent replication.
